tortuous

/TOR-choo-uhs/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Tortuous means full of twists and turns.

Lost tourists often give up on the old quarter's tortuous cobblestone alleys, which bend, fork, and loop back on themselves every few steps.

Example

The trail through the slot canyon was so tortuous that hikers lost sight of one another around every bend, and the route folded through a dozen tight turns in a single mile.

The trail constantly bends, folds, and turns rather than running straight, so hikers can never see far ahead. A path defined by that endless twisting is exactly what tortuous describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

winding: Winding means curving gently along its course, the way a river winds through a valley; the curves are easy, even pleasant. Tortuous means twisting relentlessly, tight turn after tight turn, until the twisting itself becomes the obstacle.

serpentine: Serpentine means twisting like a snake, in smooth, continuous S-curves, and the word often admires the shape, as in a serpentine garden path. Tortuous has no admiration in it: a tortuous route twists so constantly and so tightly that following it becomes a trial.

meandering: Meandering means following a slow, wandering course with no hurry and no plan, like a meandering stream or a meandering conversation; the word is relaxed. Tortuous is punishing: its endless tight turns and doubling back frustrate anyone actually trying to get somewhere.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

straight: extending without bends or curves

direct: going the shortest way, without detours

Where it sits · how tangled the route becomes

crooked → tortuous → labyrinthine

crooked vs. tortuous: A crooked path has a few bends in it; a tortuous one twists and turns constantly along its whole length.

labyrinthine vs. tortuous: A labyrinthine route is even more extreme than a tortuous one, so tangled that it feels like a maze designed to trap you.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — tort: to twist (Latin torquere, tortus)

Suffix — -uous: full of, characterized by

Put it together: The Latin root tort means 'to twist,' and the suffix -uous means 'full of.' Put together, tortuous literally means 'full of twists,' which is exactly how it describes a winding road or path.

Use the root in a new word: contort: The gymnast could contort her body into positions that made the audience wince.

Root Check

Word Choice

Neutral / descriptive

Tortuous usually describes routes: a tortuous road, path, river, or trail. Be careful not to confuse it with torturous, which means 'causing torture or great pain'; a tortuous lane merely twists, while a torturous hike leaves you in agony. Tortuous can also describe overly complicated arguments or procedures, but its core image is always literal winding.
